title: "Quantization"
description: "Representing model values with lower-precision numbers to reduce storage or computation cost."
term: "Quantization"
letter: "Q"

difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

Quantization stores or computes numbers using fewer bits. In machine
learning, this can shrink model weights and sometimes speed up inference,
with a possible trade-off in numerical accuracy.

## Technical explanation

Quantization maps values from a higher-precision range to a finite set of
lower-precision levels. Affine quantization commonly uses a scale and zero
point to map between floating-point and integer values. Methods include
post-training quantization and quantization-aware training.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Lower-precision representations can reduce model memory, bandwidth, and
hardware cost, enabling deployment on constrained devices or higher
throughput. The benefit depends on supported kernels, model architecture,
and acceptable quality loss.

## How it works

A quantizer scales and rounds values to representable levels; inference
performs operations in a supported low-precision format or converts values
when needed. Calibration can estimate activation ranges, while
quantization-aware training simulates quantization effects during learning.

## Practical example

A team can quantize a trained model to an 8-bit format, run it on the target
device, and compare task metrics, memory use, and end-to-end latency with the
floating-point baseline. Tests should include representative edge cases.

## Common misconceptions

- Quantization does not always improve latency; hardware and runtime support
  determine whether operations are faster.
- A lower bit-width does not imply a fixed amount of accuracy loss for every
  model or task.
